notes.short: “Gouge it out”: cut off whatever leads to sin
notes.about: Jesus says that if your right eye causes you to sin, you should “gouge it out and throw it away.” He is not asking anyone to harm the body. The command says more than is meant literally, to teach that even what is dearest must be given up if it leads into sin.

figure.words: gouge it out and throw it away
figure.means: give up whatever leads you into sin, however dear it is, at any cost

notes.short: The eye, the body's lamp, pictures the inner light
notes.about: Jesus draws a likeness from the body: the eye is its lamp, and a good eye fills the whole body with light, while a bad one leaves it dark. As the eye guides the body, so the mind's inner eye guides the whole life; and if that light is darkness, “how great is that darkness!”

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: The eye is the lamp of the body
figure.means: the mind's inner eye, which guides the whole life as the eye guides the body: clear and set on God, it fills life with light; darkened, it leaves all dark

original.note: In Matthew's Greek the good eye is haplous, single or clear: an eye that does not look two ways.

notes.evidence: Chrysostom, in Thomas Aquinas' Catena Aurea, calls it a parable of the bodily members: what the eye is to the body, the understanding is to the soul. notes.short: A saying: the mouth speaks what fills the heart
notes.about: Rebuking the Pharisees, Jesus uses a short saying that may later have come into common use: what fills the heart comes out in speech. Their evil words against Him showed the malice in their hearts. Luke 6:45 gives the same saying.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks
figure.means: what fills a person's heart comes out in what he says; here the Pharisees' evil words show their evil hearts

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists the words under Parœmia, among proverbs that first appear in Scripture and have since passed into general use. Calvin treats them as a proverbial saying that states what usually happens, not an invariable rule, since a cruel man may deceive with flattery, and says Christ reproaches the Pharisees with showing by their words the malice they had conceived within.
notes.limit: One writer lists the words among sayings first found in Scripture that later came into common use. The other notes that a saying like this tells what usually happens, not a rule without exception: an evil man can sometimes speak fair words.

notes.short: Jonah in the fish points to Jesus in the grave
notes.about: Jesus Himself sets Jonah beside His own burial and rising. As Jonah spent three days and three nights in the great fish and came out alive, so the Son of Man would lie in the earth and rise again. This is “the sign of the prophet Jonah,” pointing ahead to His resurrection.

figure.name: Type
figure.words: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish
figure.means: Jonah, swallowed and then brought out alive, pointing ahead to Jesus' burial and His rising from the dead

notes.evidence: Benson: Jonah was herein a type of Christ. Henry: the grave was to Christ as the fish's belly to Jonah; as Jonah came out, Christ would rise. Barnes: as Jonah was restored alive, so He would be raised. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls Jonah's case analogous, reversed in three days. Calvin keeps the likeness to one point: risen, He would speak to them, as Jonah came up to Nineveh.
notes.limit: The likeness is not pressed at every point. One reading keeps it to one: that He would die, rise and speak to them again, as Jonah came up from the sea and preached at Nineveh.

notes.short: A spirit's return pictures “this wicked generation”
notes.about: Jesus tells of an unclean spirit that leaves a man and finds no rest. It comes back to find the house vacant and swept clean, then brings seven spirits worse than itself. The man ends worse than he began. The last words apply the picture: “So will it be with this wicked generation.”

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: When an unclean spirit comes out of a man
figure.means: that generation: though it was reformed for a time, its evil would come back and its end be worse than before

Barnes says the man's state pictured that generation, which, though reformed outwardly, would go back and grow worse. Clarke says Jesus used the case to show the real state of the Jewish people.

notes.short: Seed on four soils: the word in different hearts
notes.about: Jesus tells of a farmer whose seed falls on four kinds of ground, and only the good soil bears a crop. He explains it Himself in verses 18-23: the seed is “the message of the kingdom”, and the soils are its hearers, fruitful only in the one who “hears the word and understands it”.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: A farmer went out to sow his seed
figure.means: the message of the kingdom, sown in hearers whose hearts receive it in different ways, so that only some bear fruit

original.note: In Matthew's Greek “parables” is parabolē, from words for setting one thing beside another: a comparison.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry reads the seed as the word of the kingdom and the ground as hearts disposed in different ways. Albert Barnes calls the sowing an illustration of preaching the gospel. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) titles it the effect of the word depending on the state of the heart. Adam Clarke explains Matthew's Greek word as a comparison and says few hearers would bear fruit.
notes.limit: The note does not press the four grounds to tell how many hearers bear fruit.

notes.short: Wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest
notes.about: Jesus likens the kingdom to a man who sows good seed; an enemy sows weeds among the wheat, and the owner lets both grow until the harvest. He explains it in verses 36-43: the sower is the Son of Man, the weeds are “the sons of the evil one”, and at the end of the age the angels weed out the wicked.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field
figure.means: the sons of the kingdom, sown by the Son of Man, and the sons of the evil one, sown by the devil, left to grow together until the end of the age

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry takes the good seed as true saints and the weeds as the wicked, mixed together in this world. Albert Barnes says the two must remain together until the end, when they are separated. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) places the weeds in the visible church and the separation at Christ's coming. John Calvin sees bad men mingled with the good while the church is in this world.
notes.limit: Jesus says “The field is the world” (verse 38); most of the writers apply the mixture to false members within the visible church.

notes.short: The smallest of seeds becomes a tree
notes.about: Jesus likens the kingdom to a mustard seed that a man plants in his field. It is the smallest of seeds, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree where the birds nest. The kingdom begins small and grows great.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man planted in his field
figure.means: the gospel and the kingdom of God: weak and small at its beginning, it grows until it spreads through the world, as grace also grows in the heart

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says it shows the gospel's small beginnings and great increase, in the church and in the heart. John Calvin says Christ encourages His disciples not to stumble at the Gospel's mean beginnings. Albert Barnes calls seed and plant an apt illustration of the church's progress. David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) names its subject: the kingdom's growth from the smallest beginnings.
notes.limit: Two of the writers apply it both to the church in the world and to grace growing in one heart.

notes.short: A little leaven works through all the flour
notes.about: Jesus likens the kingdom to leaven that a woman mixes into three measures of flour until all of it is leavened. Hidden in the dough, the leaven works through the whole, as the gospel works from within, in hearts and through the world.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour
figure.means: the gospel, working silently and steadily from within until it reaches the whole soul and all the nations

notes.short: Treasure in a field, worth selling all to buy
notes.about: Jesus likens the kingdom to treasure hidden in a field. A man finds it, hides it again, and in his joy sells all he has to buy that field. The kingdom is worth more than all a person owns, and worth giving up all for, with joy.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field
figure.means: the kingdom and the gospel, worth more than the whole world, to be gladly preferred to everything that would keep a person from it

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says this parable and the next show the kingdom of great value, and makes Christ the treasure, hid in the gospel. figure.means: the kingdom, Christ in the gospel, worth more than all else, so that whoever truly finds it will part with everything to have it

notes.short: A net gathers every kind, and the catch is sorted
notes.about: Jesus likens the kingdom to a net cast into the sea that gathers fish of every kind; once it is drawn ashore, the good are kept and the bad thrown away. He explains it in verses 49-50: at the end of the age the angels will “separate the wicked from the righteous”.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was cast into the sea
figure.means: the gospel gathering people of every kind, true and false, until the angels separate the wicked from the righteous at the end of the age

original.note: In Matthew's Greek the net is a sagēnē, a big dragnet that sweeps up all in its path.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry reads the net as the preaching of the gospel, with hypocrites and true Christians parted when it is drawn ashore. Albert Barnes says the gospel gathers good and bad until the end of the world. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) explains the word as a dragnet, showing the Gospel's far reach. John Calvin sees in it the church's present mixture of the good with the bad.
notes.limit: Some of the writers say it teaches what the parable of the weeds teaches. One also finds a warning in it: being gathered in is not enough unless one is truly His.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old
figure.means: the teacher well taught in the kingdom, who keeps a store of truth, old and new, and gives out of it what each hearer needs

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls it the parable of the good householder, which rivets all the rest, and Albert Barnes another parable; Joseph Benson calls it a similitude. With John Calvin, who says Jesus likens teachers to householders with a store laid up for others, they read it as the taught disciple bringing out his store of truth for the good of his hearers.
notes.limit: The writers differ on the new and the old. Two take them as truth from the Old Testament and the New; one thinks that forced and takes them as teaching varied to fit each hearer.

cites.quote: Here is the parable of the good householder, which is intended to rivet all the rest. ... He compares them to a good householder, who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old ... What should be a minister's furniture, a treasure of things new and old. ... truths new and old, out of the Old Testament and out of the new ... laying up is in order to laying out, for the benefit of others.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He enjoined on them their duty to make a proper use of this knowledge by speaking another parable. ... They should bring it forth in due time, like a householder bringing out of his treasury ... what had been laid up there ... The truth, new or old, which you have gained, keep it not laid up and hid, but bring it forth, in due season and on proper occasions, to benefit others.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: By this similitude our Lord showed his disciples the use they were to make of the knowledge they had acquired, whether from the old revelation ... or from the new one of which Jesus was the author and dispenser. ... just so every able minister of the gospel, out of the stores of his knowledge, must bring forth instructions suitable to the necessities of his hearers.

Many of the ancient expositors understand by things new and old the Law and the Gospel; but this appears to me to be forced. I understand them simply to mean a varied and manifold distribution, wisely and properly adapted to the capacity of every individual.

notes.short: The hometown's questions turn back on themselves
notes.about: The account goes out and comes back: His hometown, their astonishment, where He got this wisdom, His father and mother; then His brothers and sisters, where He got all this, their offense, and a prophet without honor in his hometown.

lines.words: Coming to His hometown, He taught the people in their synagogue,
and they were astonished.
Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?
Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary,
and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas?
Where then did this man get all these things?
And they took offense at Him.
Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor.

notes.evidence: Boys sets out these verses in eight parts, the first and last answering each other in two ways, as the two at the centre do. Next stand the people astonished, then offended; then their two questions; and at the centre His father and mother, then His brothers and sisters.

cites.quote: Here, in D., we have the father and mother of Christ; in D., his brethren and sisters: … In C. and C., we have the corresponding inquiries, … in B., the people “astonished” at Jesus; in B., “offended in him.” In A. and A., the extreme members, the correspondence is two-fold, as it is in the central ones

notes.short: A saying: a prophet is not honored at home
notes.about: When His hometown takes offense at Him, Jesus answers with a saying that seems to have been in common use: a prophet is honored least by those who know him best. His own town proved it true of Him. Mark 6:4 and John 4:44 give it too.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor
figure.means: a man God sends is less esteemed by those who knew him growing up than by strangers; Jesus applies it to His own town

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists the words under Parœmia, among proverbs first found in Scripture and since in general use. Clarke and Barnes say they seem to have been a proverbial expression, true in general; Calvin allows it may be a general proverb, which Christ turns on His Galilean countrymen; Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) says the proverb seems to have been often on His lips.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether it was already a saying: some suggest it was, while one lists it among sayings first found in Scripture. It is given as a general truth, not a rule without exception; in Jesus' own town it held true.

notes.about: The first line asks why they break the command of God, and the last says they nullify the word of God, both for the sake of their tradition. if anyone says to his father or mother,

notes.short: Plants stand for people God did not plant
notes.about: Told that the Pharisees were offended, Jesus speaks only of plants His Father did not plant, which will be pulled up. He does not say whom He means. Many read the plants as the Pharisees and all like them whose religion is not God's own work. Next He says, “Disregard them! They are blind guides.”

figure.words: Every plant
figure.means: people, such as the Pharisees, whose religion God did not plant, and who will be pulled up

notes.limit: Some have taken the plants to be the teachings of men rather than the men; one writer rejects that, and others take in both the men and what they taught.

notes.short: “The dogs” points to the Gentile woman, unnamed
notes.about: Jesus does not tell the Canaanite woman that she is a dog. He speaks only of the children's bread and the dogs, and leaves her to see that she, a Gentile, is meant. She takes the point and answers in faith, and He tells her, “your faith is great!” (verse 28).

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.words: dogs
figure.means: the woman herself, as a Gentile, whom Jesus does not name

original.note: In Matthew's Greek the word is kunarion, a little dog.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hypocatastasis: Jesus left out all mention of her and put a dog in her place. Calvin says He compares the woman herself to a dog; Henry, that He pressed the name for Gentiles against her; Clarke and Barnes, that He used the common name for Gentiles, Barnes adding, to test her faith; E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary), a house dog, marking Israel's prior claim.
notes.limit: The writers differ on the tone. One hears a harsh, disdainful word, though spoken to test her faith. Others say Jesus used a name then in common use, and one that its small form was gentler, with no scorn meant.

notes.about: After His silence and His hard answer, Jesus' reply to the Canaanite woman breaks out as a cry: “O woman,” and “your faith is great!” The words show His warm, admiring praise of a faith that kept on asking, and He grants her request.

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.words: your faith is great!
figure.means: Jesus' warm, admiring praise of her faith, after His silence and refusal

Henry says Christ, who had hidden His face from her, now gathers her with kindness, speaks like Himself and commends her faith.

notes.short: “Leaven” stands for teaching Jesus leaves unnamed
notes.about: Jesus warns of leaven without saying what He means, and the disciples think He is talking about bread. Only after His rebuke do they see He meant “the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (verse 12). Many read the picture as showing how such teaching spreads, as leaven works through dough.

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.words: leaven
figure.means: the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees, as verse 12 explains

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hypocatastasis: Jesus implies the word doctrine and never says it. notes.limit: Some of these writers take the leaven to cover the hypocrisy and worldly life that went with the teaching as well; Luke 12:1 calls the leaven of the Pharisees hypocrisy.

figure.words: O unbelieving and perverse generation!
figure.means: Jesus' grieved rebuke of the unbelief around Him

notes.short: A little child set among the disciples

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: Jesus invited a little child to stand among them
figure.means: humility: they must become lowly like a child, who seeks no rank above others, for that is true greatness in His kingdom

notes.limit: The likeness lies in humility, as Jesus explains it in verse 4. It does not make children a pattern in every way.

notes.short: One sheep strays, and the owner searches for it
notes.about: Jesus warns against looking down on these little ones, then asks what a man does when one of his hundred sheep goes astray: he leaves the ninety-nine to search for it, and rejoices to find it. Verse 14 applies it: “your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray
figure.means: God the Father, who seeks His straying little ones and rejoices to find them, so that none of them is to be despised or lost

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes: a parable on why Christians must not be despised, for God seeks and rejoices over one restored. John Calvin: we must bear with Christ's straying sheep and bring them back. David Brown (JFB): it shows how loath He is to lose one. Matthew Henry: a comparison of the Father's care for them. Chrysostom (Thomas Aquinas' Catena Aurea): a parable of the Father seeking men's salvation.
notes.limit: Luke 15:4-7 tells a like story to answer those who grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners; here it is told about the little ones. The note does not say whom the ninety-nine stand for.

notes.short: Not willing that they perish: He wills them saved
notes.about: Jesus says the Father is not willing that any of these little ones should perish. The words say less than they mean: the Father does more than not want them lost; He wills that they be saved.

figure.words: is not willing that any of these little ones should perish

notes.short: A homeowner who would have watched for the thief
notes.about: Jesus pictures a homeowner: had he known in which watch of the night the thief would come, he would have stayed awake and kept his house from being broken into. He draws the lesson at once: “you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: If the homeowner had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming
figure.means: the coming of the Son of Man, as sudden and unannounced as a thief’s, which calls His people to be ready at all times

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it another similitude: one who hears robbers are about cannot sleep, and Christ will come as suddenly as a robber, so we must always watch. Henry calls it a particular instance, the house being our own souls. Barnes: a man would be ready for a robber, and Christ will come as suddenly. Jerome, in the Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas, says the instance shows why the day is kept secret.
notes.limit: The likeness lies in the suddenness of His coming, without warning, not in any likeness of Christ to a thief.

notes.short: Ten virgins, five ready and five not
notes.about: Jesus likens the kingdom at His coming to ten virgins who wait with lamps for the bridegroom. The five wise take extra oil; the five foolish do not. When he comes, those who are ready go in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door is shut. He applies it: “Therefore keep watch.”

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom
figure.means: Christ’s coming as the Bridegroom: all who profess His name wait for Him, but only those truly ready when He comes go in with Him

notes.evidence: Henry calls it a similitude: the Bridegroom is Christ, the virgins those who profess His name, the wise sincere and the foolish hypocrites. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says it shows the watchful, expectant faith of believers. Calvin: one must persevere to the end. Plumptre (Ellicott) reads the oil as grace, the gift of the Holy Spirit. Barnes sees Christ’s coming pictured as a marriage.
notes.limit: The writers agree on its call to be ready for His coming; only some of them give a meaning to details such as the lamps and the oil.

notes.short: Servants trusted with talents give account
notes.about: A man going on a journey entrusts his money to his servants, each by his ability. Two put it to work and double it; the third hides his in the ground. On his return the master rewards the faithful two and casts out the lazy one. Many read the master as Christ, who will call His servants to account.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: it is just like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted them with his possessions
figure.means: Christ, who goes away and entrusts His servants with His gifts, and at His return calls each to account for how he used them

original.note: In Matthew's Greek a talent is a sum of money, not a gift or skill. The later use of the word for a person's gifts grew out of this parable.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls it the parable of the talents, with Christ as the Master and Christians as the servants. Albert Barnes says it shows how He will deal with people at His return. David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) reads the goods as all their gifts. Joseph Benson says it urges diligence until the Lord comes. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) takes the talents as opportunities.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the talents stand for: some take them as gifts and abilities of every kind, while one takes them less as natural gifts than as opportunities, such as possessions and offices.

notes.short: As a shepherd parts the sheep from the goats
notes.about: Jesus says that when He comes in glory the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, the sheep on His right and the goats on His left. The good and the wicked, who now live mixed together, will then be parted.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats
figure.means: the King parting the righteous from the wicked at His coming; those who now live mixed together in one flock will then be set apart

notes.evidence: John Calvin calls it a comparison: the wicked now live mixed with the good in God's flock until that day. Matthew Henry counts the parting of the sheep and goats among the passage's parabolical parts and calls Christ the great Shepherd. Joseph Benson takes the sheep as the righteous and the goats as the wicked. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) sees the shepherd parting them in judgment.
notes.limit: The note claims only the likeness of the shepherd. One of the writers says plainly that the scene as a whole is a picture of the last judgment rather than a parable.
